display_title: Esophageal GIST management: a 23-patient retrospective series
summary: A single-center series describes endoscopic, surgical and conservative management of 23 patients with esophageal GIST. Treatment selection, postoperative events and follow-up are descriptive observations, without randomized comparison or proof that one approach improves survival.
research_question: What treatment approaches and clinical follow-up were reported in a single-center series of patients with esophageal GIST, and what can this small, selected cohort establish?
author_summary: The investigators reviewed 23 patients with pathologically confirmed esophageal GIST. Fifteen underwent endoscopic resection, five direct surgery, two surgery after neoadjuvant imatinib, and one conservative treatment. The endoscopic procedures comprised nine STER, four ESD and two EMBL; 12 of these 15 tumors were reported as no larger than 30 mm. Paroxysmal palpitations and fever were each reported once after endoscopic treatment. Mean follow-up was 48.2 ± 24.2 months; one described patient developed recurrence at 15 months and died at 29 months. Procedure choice depended on clinical and tumor features. These observations illustrate a center’s treatment experience and do not establish comparative safety, survival benefit, or a validated treatment-selection rule. The inconsistent enrollment cutoff and mitotic-index wording are retained as reporting limitations, without choosing a correction.

key_findings.claim: The endoscopic group had two reported postoperative adverse events: one episode of paroxysmal palpitations and one of fever.
key_findings.context: The denominator is the 15 endoscopically treated patients. The article describes management of both events, but this small, selected retrospective group cannot establish lower treatment risk than surgery.

key_findings.claim: The article reports mean follow-up of 48.2 months and documents one patient with postoperative recurrence at 15 months and death at 29 months.
key_findings.context: The follow-up mean covers the reported series. The recurrence and death times describe patient No. 16, not a model-derived survival estimate. A separate account of patient No. 21 concerns a previous, incompletely documented procedure; it is not combined into a new recurrence-rate calculation.

what_this_adds: A documented 23-patient treatment series spanning endoscopic resection, direct surgery, surgery after neoadjuvant imatinib and conservative management.
Procedure-specific descriptive experience that separates selected clinical observations from comparative efficacy claims.

supports: The reported 23-patient case series and its mutually exclusive treatment allocations.
The three endoscopic techniques, lesion-size distribution, reported endoscopic events and specific follow-up observations.
Discussion of how clinician-selected case mix limits comparisons between endoscopic and surgical approaches.
does_not_establish: Superior safety, survival or oncologic equivalence of endoscopy versus surgery.
A validated universal size cutoff, treatment algorithm or replacement for clinical guidelines.
A causal effect of imatinib or any procedure on recurrence or survival.
Prospective, multicenter or externally validated outcomes.
A reconciled 2023 enrollment cutoff or corrected mitotic-index category.

qa.question: How many independent patients were included?
qa.answer: The single-center series reports 23 patients. The endoscopic, direct-surgery, neoadjuvant-plus-surgery and conservative groups are subdivisions of those same patients.

qa.question: How were treatment approaches distributed?
qa.answer: There were 15 endoscopic resections, five direct operations, two operations after neoadjuvant imatinib, and one conservatively managed patient. The surgical total of seven already includes the two neoadjuvant-treated patients.

qa.question: What endoscopic procedures and lesion sizes were reported?
qa.answer: The 15 endoscopic procedures included nine STER, four ESD and two EMBL. Twelve tumors in this group were reported as no larger than 30 mm. This selected experience does not validate a universal treatment cutoff.

qa.question: Does the study show that endoscopy is safer or more effective than surgery?
qa.answer: No. Clinicians selected treatment according to tumor and patient features, and the groups differed in case mix. Two reported endoscopic adverse events in a small retrospective sample do not establish comparative safety or survival benefit.

qa.question: What follow-up observation can be cited?
qa.answer: The reported mean follow-up was 48.2 ± 24.2 months. Patient No. 16 developed recurrence at 15 months after surgery and died at 29 months. These observations are not a randomized treatment effect or a validated survival prediction.

limitations: The study is retrospective and includes 23 patients at one center. Treatment was chosen by experienced clinicians on the basis of tumor size, location, origin and growth pattern, creating strong selection differences between treatment groups.

No randomized comparison, adjusted treatment-effect estimate or external validation establishes superiority or oncologic equivalence. The discussion’s procedural suggestions are not independently validated selection rules.
The abstract and Methods 2.1 specify January 2017 to August 2023, whereas Results 3.1 says January 2017 to December 2023. No exact corrected end date is adopted.
Results 3.2 describes the highest mitotic-index category as >5/50 HPF, while Table 2 labels it >10/50 HPF. This category is excluded from the quantitative findings rather than silently corrected.

The manuscript discusses an earlier procedure and suspected recurrence in patient No. 21 without the original postoperative pathology. It is not used to derive an additional event rate, survival curve or effect estimate.

Postoperative adverse-event counts and follow-up are reported observations in small selected groups. No unreported confidence interval, standardized quality-of-life score or recurrence-rate estimate is generated.

The complete six-page publisher-layout PDF was reviewed. It contains no identified supplementary-results appendix or supplementary-file citation needed for the findings reproduced here; this does not assert that no supplementary resource exists elsewhere.

related_papers.relationship: A separate reported comparison of endoscopic and laparoscopic resection at the esophagogastric junction. Differences in site, design and unresolved cohort accounting mean it is not treated as independent validation or pooled with this series.

provenance.version: Six-page publisher-layout journal article, European Journal of Surgical Oncology 50 (2024), 108527; available online 1 July 2024. Title, DOI, eleven-author order and journal identity agree with the formal PubMed and archived Crossref records.
provenance.evidence_basis: Full text through references reviewed; Tables 1–3 and Figure 3 visually checked. Numeric claims are restricted to internally consistent descriptive counts and specifically attributed follow-up observations.
provenance.uploader: Shanshan Zhu; ResearchGate Private Full-text file dated 23 April 2025.
provenance.acquired_format: E-GIST.pdf, six readable PDF pages, acquired through an authorized ResearchGate author-account download.
provenance.license: Copyright 2024 Elsevier Ltd, BASO and the European Society of Surgical Oncology. No open redistribution licence is asserted; the PDF remains in the private audit directory and is not distributed by the website.
provenance.reporting_discrepancies: Enrollment cutoff August versus December 2023; highest mitotic-index category >5/50 HPF in text versus >10/50 HPF in Table 2. Neither discrepancy is silently corrected.
